en: The national flower, Sampaguita, is a species of jasmine whose white petals open at night and release a strong fragrance to attract pollinating moths.
Ifugao farmers build stone-walled rice terraces that follow the natural contour lines of the mountains to prevent soil erosion and capture rainwater.
Dr. Ramon Barba discovered that spraying potassium nitrate on mango trees induces flowering, allowing farmers to harvest fruit year-round instead of just once.
The Philippine eagle, our national bird, builds the largest nest of any bird of prey, using branches high up in old-growth dipterocarp forests.
The South Sea pearl, our national gem, forms when a giant pearl oyster secretes layers of nacre around an irritating grain of sand.
During the Pahiyas Festival, Lucban residents decorate their houses with kiping, which are brightly dyed, leaf-shaped wafers made from ground rice and natural plant extracts.
The ancient Baybayin writing system was originally carved into bamboo tubes and palm leaves using sharp styluses before the introduction of processed paper.
Dr. Angel Alcala pioneered the use of artificial coral reefs made from concrete blocks to restore fish populations in the damaged marine environments of Apo Island.
The carabao, our national animal, lacks sweat glands and cools its body by wallowing in mud and water, which also protects its skin from sunburn.
The old-growth dipterocarp forests of Mount Makiling served as a natural fortress and hiding place for Katipuneros during the Philippine revolution against Spanish colonial rule.
The traditional bayanihan practice of moving a nipa hut relies on the lightweight, flexible structural properties of bamboo poles carried by the community's men.
Abaca, our national fiber, is a banana relative whose strong leaf stalks are stripped and dried in the sun to create durable Manila hemp.
